data.why: A fire hydrant on a street sidewalk, cut open in section so the barrel, the buried valve and the main pipe show. The video opens close on the red hydrant above ground with a hand cranking it, and a tennis ball sits by the curb. Each loop adds one real hydrant part (valve, deep burial, stem, drain hole, threads, flange, caps, five-sided nut), and the camera stays on the hydrant. At the end a fire truck arrives and the hydrant works again.

sentences.text: If you crank open a fire hydrant, you have a geyser.
But the water blasts out and floods the street.
So you add a valve that shuts the flow.
But ice freezes that valve and splits it open.
So you dig down and bury the valve deep.
But the buried valve sits too far to reach.
So you add a long stem that turns the valve.
But once the stem shuts it, water stays and freezes.
So you drill a drain hole that empties the barrel.
This is a dry barrel hydrant.
But when the valve opens, water pours from the drain hole.
So you let the stem seal the hole.
Turn the nut, and water rises up the barrel.
But opening fast slams the water, and the main bursts.
So you cut threads, so the stem takes many turns.
A hydrant can push out 1,000 gallons every minute.
But a speeding car hits and snaps the hydrant.
So you add a breakaway flange that keeps it shut.
But shut again, the bare nozzle cannot hold a hose.
So you add threaded caps that a hose screws onto.
But the threaded caps stay tight and the wrench slips.
So you add a five sided nut for wrenches.
Those are the hydrants you pass every day.
Add a fire truck, open the hydrant, and water flows.
Congratulations, you have built a working hydrant.
